description: A team from Peru led by Julio Sifuentes, a Mechanical Engineer (UPC Barcelona, Industry 4.0) with international experience in mechatronics and continuous improvement, and certified in Data Science & Machine Learning. Inspired by the Pachamama, the Andean “Mother Earth”, we turn NASA Earth data into clear trends that show how our planet is changing.
summary:
Earth Trend Detective is a free web app that tells anyone whether their place is really getting hotter or drier. Pick any point on Earth and, in about a minute, it turns 45 years of NASA POWER data (1981–2025) into a one-page case file: a plain-language verdict, colour stripes of the 45 years, the rate of change per decade with a 95% range, and practical actions.

It addresses the “Earth System Trend Detective” challenge by detecting long-term trends in heat, rainfall and soil moisture, and testing them statistically with Mann-Kendall (corrected for autocorrelation) and the Sen slope. It is honest by design: it says “no evidence” when there is none and states its limits on every case file.

It matters because 2.41 billion workers are exposed to excessive heat and 4 billion people face severe water scarcity. The data is free, but local, trustworthy answers are not. Municipalities, companies with outdoor crews and farmers can now act on evidence. Built by one person with vibe coding.
details:
What it does and how it works. Earth Trend Detective is a free web app that tells anyone whether their place is really getting hotter or drier. The user picks any point on a 3D globe or map, or searches for a town. The app downloads 45 years (1981–2025) of monthly NASA POWER data and builds a one-page case file: a one-sentence verdict, a Yes / Possible / No evidence verdict for each variable, colour stripes of the 45 years, the rate of change per decade with a 95% range, and practical actions. For example, felt heat in Monzón, Peru, is rising +0.38 °C per decade.

How the analysis works. It uses six NASA variables (temperature, rainfall, soil moisture, humidity, solar energy) plus felt heat from the NOAA heat index. Trends are tested with Mann-Kendall, corrected for autocorrelation, and measured with the Sen slope and a 95% interval. We checked the heat-index code against 45 cells of the official NWS table (maximum gap 0.5 °F).

Benefits. Municipalities plan shade, alerts and rationing. Companies with outdoor crews shift heavy work to dawn. Farmers and cooperatives choose crops and irrigation. Health services, schools and NGOs can attach NASA evidence to campaigns and funding requests. It is free, needs no account or API key, and works in English and Spanish.

Intended impact. About 2.41 billion workers are exposed to excessive heat (ILO), and 4 billion people face severe water scarcity at least one month a year. The data to guide local decisions is free, but a local, plain-language, trustworthy answer is not. We aim to let any town write “page one” of its adaptation plan in a minute. Next: a pilot in Peru, heat-day counts, then forecasting.

Tools and technology. HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript in 11 modules, a static page with no backend. Globe.gl (3D globe), Leaflet (map), NASA GIBS imagery, NASA POWER API (MERRA-2, SRB/CERES), and Photon/Nominatim for place search. No special hardware: it runs in any browser. It was built by one person using vibe coding, AI pair programming with Claude.

Creativity. Instead of a dashboard of raw charts, it produces a “case file” that answers one question in plain words. It is also honest by design: it is built to say “no evidence” when there is none, which most climate tools avoid. The “since you were born” view and the place comparison make the change personal.

Factors we considered. Trust: statistical corrections and a verified heat index. Clarity: a high-school student must understand every screen. Limits, stated on every case file: about 50 km per data point, reanalysis rather than weather stations, a known jump in NASA rainfall and soil data around 2015, and it measures the past, not a forecast. Accessibility: free, no backend, two languages, open code.
